newsitem.title: UK: Russia Eurobond suffers further on Yeltsin worries.
newsitem.headline: Russia Eurobond suffers further on Yeltsin worries.

text.p: Russia's $1.0 billion Eurobond, under pressure since December, saw further price falls on fears over President Boris Yeltsin's health, traders said on Thursday.

"This time yesterday (Wednesday) Russia's Eurobond was trading around 380 basis points over Treasuries. But the news Yeltsin was back in hospital bounced it wider," an emerging market debt trader at a U.S. bank said.
After Yeltsin was taken to hospital on Wednesday with pneumonia the spread hit 411 b.p. in New York but was back around 400 b.p. today in London, he said.
Prices on other Russian debt also fell but recovered somewhat on Thursday, dealers said. Vneshekonombank dollar debt gained a point after losing 1-1/2 points in New York.

The Russian Eurobond, launched to yield 345 b.p. over U.S. Treasuries, was its first international debt issue since the 1917 revolution and set a benchmark for further sovereign deals and for other Russian borrowers.
The yield spread began an upward climb in mid-December to trade between 380 and 390 b.p. over, dealers said.
"It started off very well. The marketing was well done and the Russians presented themselves well," said an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"I would have capped the amount at $750 million. Sometimes the last $250 million can be a bridge too far," he said.
Other bankers said the widening reflected investors pulling out of the market before the end of the year and, as money flowed back to the sector, it would come in again.
"Before Yeltsin, we already saw the Eurobond tighten by around 10 b.p. this year. There is plenty of money coming into emerging markets," said a Russian debt trader.
"Russia was a mega-hyped deal. Many froth accounts bought the paper in November but wanted to be flat over Christmas because the market is then illiquid and sold," he said.
He expected the spread to rally to around 310 b.p. in three months' time.
For spread players Russia's Eurobond now looked a good buy, another trader said.

"A relatively attractive Eurobond, especially for European investors, has become more attractive (now the spread is wider)," said Eric Fine, Russian fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley in London.
"A 400 b.p. spread for a double-B credit is cheap. I think three or four months from now this bond will be tighter, perhaps dramatically tighter," he said.
Such a move would bode well for Russia's next venture into the bond markets, which is expected to take the form of a jumbo mark Eurobond.
"A mark deal will be compared with the dollar deal, so where that is trading is very important," said a U.S. bank trader.
The Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist said: "You cannot fully ignore the developments in the dollar market when pricing a mark Eurobond."
